The Structure of Zeros

Theory, Chapter 4

theory-04-the-structure-of-zeros.Rmd

What a zero means

When a species has zero cover in a plot, the species is not there. A statement about the world: this species does not occupy any portion of this plot.

This interpretation has consequences. A zero is not a small positive value that happens to be recorded as zero. Categorically different. A species with 0.1% cover is present; a species with 0% cover is absent. The distinction between presence and absence is not a matter of precision. A distinction in kind.

In constrained intensity data more broadly (market shares, time allocations, compositional mixtures) zeros carry the same meaning. A zero component indicates that the corresponding category contributes nothing to the total. It asserts something exact.

Zeros are boundary values

The simplex \(\mathcal{S}^{K-1}\) is a bounded space. Its interior consists of compositions where every component is strictly positive. Its boundary consists of compositions where at least one component equals zero.

When a species is absent from a plot, the observed composition lies on the boundary of the simplex. This changes the geometry of the problem.

In the interior of the simplex, all components can vary freely subject to the sum constraint. Small perturbations in any direction are possible. On the boundary, this freedom disappears for the zero components. A component that equals zero cannot decrease further. It can only increase or remain at zero. The local geometry is different: the space of possible movements is restricted.

This asymmetry matters for probability models. Distributions on the simplex interior (like the logistic-normal) cannot place mass exactly on the boundary. They can approach it but never reach it. A composition with an exact zero has probability zero under any such distribution. The model assigns zero probability to events that occur frequently in real data.

Why zeros are not small values

A common pragmatic response to zeros is to treat them as small positive values. Add a small constant before analysis. Replace zeros with half the detection limit. Impute a value just above zero. These approaches share a common assumption: that zeros are like very small positive values, just measured imprecisely.

False for structural zeros.

Consider a species absent from a plot. Its cover is exactly zero. Under different conditions, the species could have cover anywhere from 0% to 100%. Its absence is not a statement about where it falls on a continuous scale. The species is not on that scale at all in this plot.

Adding a small constant does not recover a meaningful quantity. It creates a fictitious positive value where none exists. The resulting analysis is not an analysis of the observed data but of a modified dataset where absence has been converted to trace presence. Not a neutral modification. It changes the information content of the data, particularly in datasets where zeros dominate.

The distinction matters inferentially. A model that treats zeros as small positive values estimates parameters as if those values were observed. It attributes variance and covariance to quantities that were not measured. It behaves as if every species has some positive cover everywhere, just very small. A misrepresentation of what the data say.

The boundary changes likelihood behaviour

Probability densities on the simplex behave differently at the boundary than in the interior.

Consider the Dirichlet distribution. When concentration parameter \(\alpha_k > 1\), the density vanishes as \(y_k \to 0\). The distribution places negligible mass near the boundary for that component. When \(\alpha_k < 1\), the density is unbounded as \(y_k \to 0\), concentrating mass near zero without placing a point mass exactly at zero. When \(\alpha_k = 1\), the density is flat.

None of these behaviours places positive probability on the event \(y_k = 0\) exactly. The Dirichlet treats zero as a limit, not an outcome. For data where zeros are common and exact, this is inadequate. The model can concentrate mass arbitrarily close to zero, but it cannot represent the discrete event of absence.

The logistic-normal is worse in this respect. Because it is defined through log-ratios, it requires all components to be strictly positive. It assigns probability zero to any composition with a zero component. The boundary of the simplex is outside its support entirely.

Any continuous distribution on the simplex interior shares this limitation. Exact zeros require a different kind of probabilistic treatment, one that acknowledges the boundary as a place where mass can accumulate, not just a limit that can be approached.

Zeros interact with compositional structure

Zeros do not occur in isolation. When one component is zero, the remaining components must sum to one among themselves. The composition is effectively projected onto a lower-dimensional face of the simplex.

Consider a five-component composition where two species are absent. The three present components must sum to one. The data point lies on a two-dimensional face of the four-dimensional simplex. The dependence structure among the present components is constrained by this reduced geometry.

Implications for inference: when zeros are common, most observations lie on lower-dimensional faces of the simplex rather than in its interior. The effective dimensionality of the data varies from observation to observation, depending on which components are present. A model that treats all observations as living in the full simplex interior misrepresents the geometry of the data.

The pattern of zeros also carries information. Which species tend to be absent together? Which combinations of presences and absences occur? This structure is part of the data-generating process. A model that handles zeros only by perturbing them into positive values discards this information.

Why hurdle thinking fails here

In other contexts, zero-heavy data are modelled using hurdle or two-part models: one component determines whether the outcome is zero or positive, another component models the positive values. Natural for count data or continuous outcomes that are zero-inflated.

For compositional data, naive application of this framing is inadequate.

The problem: zeros represent boundary events in a constrained space, and the constraint couples all components. A hurdle model that treats each component separately (deciding independently whether each is zero or positive, then modelling positive values independently) ignores the sum constraint. The zeros and positive values of different components are not independent decisions. They are jointly constrained.

This does not mean mixture structure is irrelevant to compositional data. On the contrary, representing exact zeros requires some form of discrete component that places mass on the boundary. But the discrete and continuous parts cannot be specified independently for each component. They must be coupled through the compositional constraint.

If species A is absent, the remaining species share the entire plot. If species A and B are both absent, the remaining species share it among fewer competitors. The decision of which species are present and the allocation of cover among present species are not separable processes. Aspects of a single compositional outcome.

A valid model for compositional data with zeros must represent both the discrete structure (which components are zero) and the continuous structure (how cover is allocated among nonzero components) in a way that respects the sum constraint throughout.

Zero dominance weakens information about dependence

In datasets where zeros are prevalent (where most species are absent from most plots) the information about dependence among components is concentrated in a small fraction of observations.

Consider estimating the dependence between species A and species B in the positive quadrant, when both are present. This dependence is only directly observable when both species occur in the same plot. If species A is present in 20% of plots and species B in 15%, co-occurrence rates depend on how presence patterns are structured. Under independence of presence, co-occurrence would be 3%; under positive association, it could be higher; under negative association, lower or even zero. Regardless of the association structure, co-occurrence will typically be rare when marginal presence rates are low.

A structural feature of zero-dominated compositional data. The dependence among components, which Chapter 2 established as fundamental, is only observable when components co-occur. When zeros dominate, co-occurrence is rare, and estimates of dependence are based on limited information.

A model that does not explicitly represent the zero structure cannot correctly quantify this limitation. It will either ignore zeros (and estimate dependence from fictitious positive values) or exclude zeros (and estimate dependence from a biased subsample). Neither approach correctly represents what the data can and cannot tell us.

What zeros require

The prevalence of exact zeros in compositional data is a defining feature that shapes what valid models can look like.

A model for zero-heavy compositions must:

  1. Place positive probability on exact zeros, not just on values approaching zero.

  2. Respect the sum constraint across both zero and nonzero components.

  3. Represent the joint structure of which components are zero and how cover is allocated among those that are not.

  4. Acknowledge that zeros reduce effective dimensionality and alter the observable dependence structure.

No purely continuous distribution on the simplex satisfies these requirements. The Dirichlet cannot represent exact zeros. The logistic-normal excludes them entirely. Any admissible model must incorporate discrete structure (mixture components, indicator variables, or equivalent machinery) to place mass on the boundary.

This vignette does not specify what that structure should be. It establishes that the structure is necessary. A framework that treats zeros as afterthoughts, or handles them through ad hoc modifications, has not engaged with the problem. It has evaded it.
